lead: One sentence can have more than one parse tree. 'I saw the man with the telescope' has two: the man holds the telescope, or the seeing is done with it. The grammar allows both, so the parser must choose using evidence beyond the grammar: rule probabilities, head words, word meanings, or a heuristic. This choice matters wherever a tree feeds another task, such as machine translation, question answering or information extraction, because a wrong attachment gives a wrong answer downstream.
prereq: You need parse trees from 3.1 and the fact that a parser returns every parse from 3.3.

blocks.text: Structural ambiguity, also called syntactic ambiguity, means one word sequence with fixed part-of-speech tags has two or more valid parse trees. No single word is unclear; the grammar itself licenses both bracketings.

Lexical ambiguity is a different fault. One word carries two senses or two categories: 'bank' is a river side or a money house, 'book' is a noun or a verb. A tagger settles the category (Unit 2) and word sense disambiguation settles the sense (Unit 4). Lexical ambiguity can create structural ambiguity: if 'book' is tagged as a verb, the sentence needs a verb phrase. But the two causes are separate, and an exam question often asks you to name which one you are looking at.

Local ambiguity means a span can be built in two ways while the parser is still reading, and only one of those survives to the end. Global ambiguity means the finished sentence has two complete trees. CYK and Earley keep every live option, so local ambiguity costs time, not correctness.

The count grows fast. For n prepositional phrases in a row, the number of attachment trees follows the Catalan numbers 1, 1, 2, 5, 14, 42, so five phrases already give 42 readings. Every extra phrase multiplies the work.

items: PP attachment. A prepositional phrase can hang from the noun phrase before it or from the verb phrase above it: 'I saw the man with the telescope', 'She ate the cake with a fork'. The two trees answer different questions: which man, or how she ate.

Coordination scope. 'Old men and women' brackets as [old [men and women]], where both are old, or as [[old men] and women], where only the men are old. A conjunction can join words, phrases or clauses, and its reach fixes the meaning.

Noun-noun compounds. 'The university cricket ground staff' nests four nouns with no marker of grouping. [university [cricket ground]] staff and [[university cricket] ground] staff describe different organisations.

Garden path. 'The horse raced past the barn fell' makes you take 'raced' as the main verb; 'fell' then forces 'raced past the barn' to be a reduced relative clause modifying 'horse'. The first reading is locally fine and globally dead, so the reader must backtrack.

blocks.text: Rule probabilities. A probabilistic CFG gives every rule a probability, and the probability of a tree is the product of its rule probabilities; the parser picks the tree with the highest product (3.5). Its weakness is that a rule such as VP → VP PP always has one probability, whatever the noun and preposition are, so the model cannot see that 'man with' and 'saw with' behave differently.

Head words. Lexicalized models condition each rule on the head word of the phrase, so the score for attaching a PP to 'man' differs from attaching it to 'saw' (3.8). This is the single strongest signal for PP attachment.

Selectional restrictions and word senses. A telescope is an instrument someone looks through, so 'seeing with a telescope' is a normal event; a man 'with a telescope' is normal possession too, so word meaning alone does not settle this one. 'The scientist watched the bacteria with a powerful microscope' does settle, because bacteria cannot own a microscope (Unit 4).

Heuristics. Low attachment means attaching the new phrase to the most recent phrase; it fails on 'The scientist watched the bacteria with a powerful microscope', where it picks the bacteria. Minimal attachment means building the fewest new nodes; it fails on 'The horse raced past the barn fell', where it commits to 'raced' as main verb. Both are guesses, not rules, and they can point to different trees for the same sentence.
Practical parsers keep an n-best list, the top few trees rather than one, and rerank them with head words, word senses or a neural model. The final tree is the reranker's choice.

figure.caption: Both trees are legal for the same string. The parser scores each with rule probabilities, then checks head words and word senses before committing to one tree.

spec.title: Resolving a PP attachment
spec.aria: One ambiguous sentence branches into two parses, which are scored, checked against word evidence, and reduced to one chosen tree.

nodes.label: Sentence
nodes.note: I saw the man with the telescope

examples.question: The sentence 'I saw the man with the telescope' is structurally ambiguous at the prepositional phrase. (a) Write both bracketings and name the reading each gives. (b) The grammar has P(VP → VP PP) = 0.6 and P(NP → NP PP) = 0.2, and every other rule used by the two parses has the same probability. Write the probability of each parse as a multiple of the shared factor and say which parse the PCFG chooses. (c) Give the ratio of the two probabilities.
steps: Locate the ambiguity: the PP 'with the telescope' can attach to the NP 'the man' or to the VP 'saw the man'. Both attachments are licensed by the context-free grammar, so the grammar does not choose.
Parse A: [S [NP I] [VP saw [NP the man [PP with the telescope]]]]. The PP sits inside the NP, so the man has the telescope.
Parse B: [S [NP I] [VP [VP saw [NP the man]] [PP with the telescope]]]. The PP sits inside the VP, so the seeing is done with the telescope.
Shared rules: S → NP VP, VP → V NP, NP → Det N, PP → P NP, plus the lexical rules. Their product is one number K, identical in both parses.
Probability of Parse A = 0.2 × K, because the only rule that differs is NP → NP PP with probability 0.2.
Probability of Parse B = 0.6 × K, because the differing rule is VP → VP PP with probability 0.6.
Compare: 0.6K > 0.2K, so Parse B wins. Ratio = 0.6 / 0.2 = 3.

Keep the loser: a reranker using word senses could still prefer Parse A next time, because a man holding a telescope is an ordinary event. Note also that low attachment, which attaches to the most recent phrase (here the NP), would pick Parse A, so the heuristic and the probability model disagree on this sentence.
examples.answer: Parse A scores 0.2K (the man has the telescope) and Parse B scores 0.6K (the seeing is done with the telescope); the PCFG chooses Parse B, which is 3 times more probable than Parse A.
examples.check:
p_np = 0.2
p_vp = 0.6
print(p_np)
print(p_vp)
print(p_vp / p_np)

traps: Calling a word with two senses 'structurally ambiguous'. A word like 'bank' gives lexical ambiguity; the tree changes only after a sense is chosen.
Assuming the highest-probability tree is the correct meaning. A PCFG scores structure with rule frequencies and knows nothing about truth, so its top tree can be the wrong reading.
Treating low attachment and minimal attachment as rules. Each is a heuristic that fails on ordinary sentences, and the two can point to different trees for the same sentence.
Confusing local with global ambiguity. A sentence can be locally ambiguous at every step of the parse and still finish with a single tree.
Thinking more grammar rules mean fewer parses. Every rule that can apply adds trees; broader coverage gives more ambiguity, not less.

quiz.q: Define structural ambiguity and lexical ambiguity in one line each.
quiz.a: Structural: one word sequence with fixed part-of-speech tags has two or more parse trees licensed by the grammar. Lexical: one word carries two senses or two categories.

quiz.q: Why can a parser not settle an ambiguous sentence using the grammar alone?
quiz.a: A CFG only says which structures are legal. Both trees come from the same rules, so the grammar gives no preference between them. Evidence from outside the rules is needed: rule probability, head words, word senses, or a heuristic.

quiz.q: A grammar gives P(NP → NP PP) = 0.5 and P(VP → VP PP) = 0.4, and all other rules are shared. For 'I saw the man with the telescope', which parse wins and by what factor?
quiz.a: The NP attachment (Parse A) wins: 0.5K against 0.4K, a factor of 0.5 / 0.4 = 1.25.

quiz.q: 'The horse raced past the barn fell.' Explain the garden path and name the heuristic that commits too early.
quiz.a: Minimal attachment builds the fewest new nodes, so 'raced' is taken as the main verb of the sentence. When 'fell' arrives there is no slot for a second main verb, and the reader must backtrack to the reading where 'raced past the barn' is a reduced relative clause modifying 'horse'.

quiz.q: Five prepositional phrases follow one another. How many attachment trees are there, and why does the number matter?
quiz.a: 42, the Catalan number for n = 5. A parser that enumerated them all would slow down sharply, so real parsers score and prune instead of listing every tree.

quiz.q: Give both bracketings of 'old men and women' and the meaning of each.
quiz.a: [old [men and women]]: the adjective covers the whole coordination, so both the men and the women are old. [[old men] and women]: only the men are old.

quiz.q: Why do practical parsers keep an n-best list instead of returning only the top tree?
quiz.a: The top tree from a PCFG is scored with rule frequencies that ignore lexical fit, so it can be the wrong reading. Keeping the next few trees lets a reranker using head words and word senses correct the choice. Downstream tasks also gain from knowing the runner-up reading.

beyond: Not for the exam. Attachment accuracy is measured by labelled attachment scores in dependency parsing, and PP attachment is a standard test case in that literature. Modern systems replace hand-written heuristics with models trained on treebank annotations plus head-word features, and they still return n-best lists and rerank. Search for 'prepositional phrase attachment', 'garden path sentences psycholinguistics' and 'n-best reranking parser' to go further. Reading about human eye-tracking during garden paths shows that people slow down at exactly the point where the parser must backtrack.
